extracted.intended_audience: press officers, public relations professionals, health journalists and science communicators producing or evaluating health-related press releases
extracted.subtask_description: A 10-criterion rubric for evaluating the completeness, accuracy, and balance of health-related press releases (adapted from HealthNewsReview.org). Each criterion is scored Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory/Not Applicable and combined into a proportion and star rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release adequately discuss the costs of the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report direct and indirect costs where relevant; avoid implying affordability without data. For treatments/tests/products, state costs or note when cost information is not yet available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release adequately quantify the benefits of the treatment/test/product/procedure (using absolute numbers, not just relative numbers)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer absolute risk reductions, numbers-needed-to-treat, or concrete outcome counts over only relative percentages. Include baseline risk where possible so readers can assess real-world impact; avoid statements that inflate perceived effect by using relative terms alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release adequately explain/quantify the harms of the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe potential adverse effects, side effects, and risks with frequency estimates when available. Do not omit or downplay harms; quantify harms in the same terms used to report benefits when possible (absolute counts/percentages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release seem to grasp the quality of the evidence (study design, sample size, limitations)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify study design (e.g., randomized trial, observational study), size, duration, and key limitations or sources of bias. Avoid overstating conclusions from preliminary, small, or non-randomized studies; note whether claims are based on surrogate outcomes or direct clinical endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease-mongering
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release commit disease-mongering (exaggerating disease prevalence/severity to expand market for treatment)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language that exaggerates prevalence, severity, or personal risk to create unnecessary fear or urgency. Put risk in context and avoid marketing tactics that pathologize normal experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding sources / Conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release identify funding sources & disclose conflicts of interest? (Modified for press releases - news stories ask about independent sources used.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name study sponsors, funders, and any financial ties of authors/researchers. Disclose industry sponsorship, employment, stock holdings, or other conflicts that could influence study design, interpretation, or messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with existing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release compare the new approach with existing alternatives?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the new intervention in context by comparing effectiveness, risks, costs, and availability with current standard treatments or approaches. Avoid implying superiority without direct comparative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release establish the availability of the product/procedure?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether the product/procedure is commercially available, in trials, limited to certain regions, or years from availability. Do not imply immediate access if regulatory approval, distribution, or production barriers remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release establish the true novelty of the approach?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether findings represent a genuinely new discovery, an incremental advance, replication, or early-stage research. Avoid hype that presents incremental or confirmatory work as revolutionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensational language / Press release reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: For news release reviews: Does the news release include unjustifiable, sensational language, including in the quotes of researchers? (For news stories: Does the story rely solely on a press release?)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid exaggerated adjectives, breathless claims, or overhyped quotes. Quotes should be accurate reflections of findings and limitations, not promotional soundbites. For journalists, do not rely exclusively on the press release—seek independent sources and the original study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring system / application notes
rubrics_metrics.description: How the rubric is applied: each criterion is scored 'Satisfactory,' 'Unsatisfactory,' or 'Not Applicable.' Total scores are expressed as proportions (e.g., 7/10) and converted to a 0–5 star rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HealthNewsReview applied this rubric to thousands of journalism stories and several hundred PR releases; use consistent interpretation across items (e.g., require absolute quantification to mark 'Benefits' satisfactory). If a criterion cannot reasonably apply to a particular release, mark 'Not Applicable' and adjust denominator when reporting proportions.
